## Findings
- F1 [nasa_stated] PSI-25, PSI-26: NASA's normal-gravity screening test for spacecraft materials (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) is not conservative: materials can keep burning at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.
- F2 [nasa_stated] PSI-25, PSI-26: Spraying suppressant locally at a flame did not put it out: the jet pulled in air and kept the flame burning, even with the ventilation airflow turned off.
- F3 [nasa_stated] PSI-25, PSI-26: Nitrogen applied to a burning sample as a suppressant could make the flame stronger, because the gas stream drew oxygen into it.
- F4 [nasa_stated] PSI-69: The flammability limit is lower in microgravity, so inert-gas suppressant standards set on Earth give less safety margin in space.
- F5 [nasa_stated] PSI-69: For heptane and methanol droplets, the lowest oxygen level that still supports burning (limiting oxygen index) was significantly lower than in normal gravity, and lower than predicted.
- F6 [nasa_stated] PSI-69: After the visible flame around a heptane droplet went out, a stable cool flame formed and kept burning. NASA calls this the most significant observation of these experiments.
- F7 [nasa_context] PSI-102, PSI-101: Smoke particles from fires in microgravity differ greatly in size from those on Earth, so a terrestrial smoke detector used in space would be looking for the wrong signature.
- F8 [from_data] PSI-98: At the same 20 cm/s airflow, the flame spreading with the flow (concurrent) burned for 420 s, while the flame spreading against it (opposed) burned for 70 s.
- F9 [from_data] PSI-99: None of the four silicone samples burned in microgravity (about 0 cm). In the 1-g comparison, two of them burned completely and one burned 7.6 cm.
- F10 [from_data] PSI-99: Both PMMA samples burned completely in 1-g but showed only about 10 cm of significant damage in microgravity. On one of them the flame stayed anchored at the base of the sample, which regressed only 0.01 to 0.04 mm/s.
- F11 [from_data] PSI-99: The cotton-fiberglass fabric (SIBAL) burned its full 29 cm length in microgravity, as it did in 1-g.
- F12 [record_stated] PSI-20: Gas flames emulating burning PMMA and Nylon kept burning steadily in microgravity with no airflow, even though shutting off ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires.
- F13 [record_stated] PSI-20: Burning without airflow continued in the elevated-oxygen atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, while the same flames in 21% oxygen went out in a short time.
- F14 [record_stated] PSI-20: The team calls the results preliminary, but they suggest NASA may want to rely more on its cone-calorimeter flammability test (Test 2), which measures the material properties that matched the microgravity flames.
- F15 [limitation] PSI-102, PSI-101: The particle samples from the first SAME flight could not be used: every electron-microscope grid came back contaminated with unidentified particles. This is one reason SAME-R reflew.
- F16 [limitation] PSI-69: In some atmospheres the droplet size at flame extinction was too small to be observed or measured with the instruments on board.
- F17 [nasa_stated] PSI-69: FLEX showed that a cool flame can keep burning for a prolonged time after the visible flame goes out, a result many researchers had thought impossible.
- F18 [nasa_context] PSI-25, PSI-26, PSI-98, PSI-99, PSI-100: For flames spreading over solid materials, the lowest oxygen level that supports burning occurs at an airflow of about 10 cm/s, the typical speed of spacecraft ventilation, where spread rate is also highest.
- F19 [nasa_context] PSI-25, PSI-26, PSI-98, PSI-99, PSI-100: At low airflow in space, a thin fuel lit in the middle spreads its flame upstream into the oncoming air, the opposite of normal gravity, where flames always spread with the buoyant flow.
- F20 [nasa_context] PSI-107, PSI-106: In low gravity, gas-jet flames start producing smoke at substantially different conditions than on Earth, contrary to earlier predictions, and their soot particles differ in size and structure.
